power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Social disconnection has been proposed as a contributing factor to the youth mental health crisis.
However, it remains unclear how social disruptions reshape social networks and their links to mental wellbeing across age groups.

The present study examined whether social disruptions (during the COVID-19 pandemic) reshape social networks and how changes in social networks differently relate to mental health and loneliness in adolescents compared to adults.

The study used egocentric network analysis of data from 1,278 participants (88% female; aged 11-89 years, mean = 37.2±16.2 years) in the multinational (Australia, the U.K., and U.S.) prospective COVID-19 Risks Across the Lifespan (CORAL) Study.
Social network properties of structural density, functional closeness, and interaction frequency were derived.
Linear mixed-effects modelling was employed to examine cross-sectional and prospective associations with mental wellbeing at baseline, three-month, and six-month follow-up.
Results: Adolescents reported more virtual interactions, and less in-person contact.
Greater network closeness was associated with lower depression, whereas dense but less close networks were linked to greater loneliness.
Reduced contact from pre-pandemic levels were also linked to poorer wellbeing, particularly among younger individuals.

The present findings highlight that age differences in social experiences, such as social network structure (density) and function (closeness and interaction frequency), may underlie young people's greater mental health vulnerability during social disruptions.
This underscores the importance of developing age-sensitive and context-responsive strategies to better support mental wellbeing during times of social disruption.
The global decline in youth mental health over the past two decades underscores the need to identify prevention and intervention targets (Keyes & Platt, 2024; McGorry et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The global decline in youth mental health over the past two decades underscores the need to identify prevention and intervention targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Keyes & Platt, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">McGorry et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: While a myriad of factors likely contribute to the youth mental health crisis, growing attention has focused on social connectivity and the lack thereof in young people today (Birrell et al., 2025; Holt-Lunstad & Sine, 2025).
text.formatted: While a myriad of factors likely contribute to the youth mental health crisis, growing attention has focused on social connectivity and the lack thereof in young people today <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Birrell et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Holt-Lunstad & Sine, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Social connection is a fundamental human need that promotes psychological wellbeing (Baumeister & Leary, 1995). Adolescence (11-24 years; Sawyer et al., 2018), represents a pivotal developmental period when individuals increasingly foster new, independent social connections while transitioning into adulthood (Lam et al., 2014; Pfeifer & Berkman, 2018).
text.formatted: Social connection is a fundamental human need that promotes psychological wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baumeister & Leary, 1995)</ref>. <ref type="bibr">Adolescence (11-24 years;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sawyer et al., 2018)</ref>, represents a pivotal developmental period when individuals increasingly foster new, independent social connections while transitioning into adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Lam et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Pfeifer & Berkman, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Disruptions or changes in social connections and mental health during adolescence are particularly detrimental to development and mental health (Orben et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Disruptions or changes in social connections and mental health during adolescence are particularly detrimental to development and mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Orben et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The COVID-19 pandemic, which imposed widespread physical social restrictions, offers a unique naturalistic research opportunity to investigate how changes in social connections relate to mental health across the lifespan.
During the pandemic, increased self-reported loneliness was consistently associated with poorer mental health in young people (Cooper et al., 2021; Ernst et al., 2022).
text.formatted: During the pandemic, increased self-reported loneliness was consistently associated with poorer mental health in young people <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cooper et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Ernst et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Whilst disruptions to social connection may have directly contributed to increased loneliness, they may have also led to decreased mental health by preventing young people from engaging in developmentally typical behaviours involving exploration and learning with/about their peers (Towner et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Whilst disruptions to social connection may have directly contributed to increased loneliness, they may have also led to decreased mental health by preventing young people from engaging in developmentally typical behaviours involving exploration and learning with/about their peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Towner et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This may also partially explain the greater detrimental impact of the pandemic on adolescent mental health and loneliness than on adults .
The current study therefore investigated whether and how changes in social connections were differentially related to self-perceived loneliness and mental health in adolescents and adults.
Social network data provide an ecologically-valid measure of social connections by mapping social relationships and tracking changes over time (Rassaby et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Social network data provide an ecologically-valid measure of social connections by mapping social relationships and tracking changes over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Rassaby et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Social network analysis quantifies individual's social ties, and their structural (e.g., density index which measures how close-knit a network is) and functional characteristics (e.g., emotional closeness within a network) (Burgette et al., 2021; Mehrpour et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Social network analysis quantifies individual's social ties, and their structural (e.g., density index which measures how close-knit a network is) and functional characteristics (e.g., emotional closeness within a network) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Burgette et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Mehrpour et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While scarce, research during the pandemic showed that more cohesive networks and (emotionally) stronger relationships were associated with fewer depressive symptoms (Perry et al., 2024).
text.formatted: While scarce, research during the pandemic showed that more cohesive networks and (emotionally) stronger relationships were associated with fewer depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Perry et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these effects were more pronounced in adolescents than adults (Elmer et al., 2020; Perry et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Importantly, these effects were more pronounced in adolescents than adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Elmer et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Perry et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond structural and functional changes, greater reductions in social interaction frequency, were also associated with elevated depressive symptoms during the pandemic (Sommerlad et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Beyond structural and functional changes, greater reductions in social interaction frequency, were also associated with elevated depressive symptoms during the pandemic <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Sommerlad et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These findings support social network analysis and contact-frequency as rigorous approaches to studying associations between (disrupted) social connection and mental health.
The mode of social contact should also be considered.
Technological advances have reshaped social interactions, with the expansion of digital communications further accelerating during the pandemic (Nguyen et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Technological advances have reshaped social interactions, with the expansion of digital communications further accelerating during the pandemic <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Nguyen et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Unique affordances of digital social connection (e.g., impoverished social cues, delayed feedback) have been proposed to confer greater mental health risks, particularly among adolescents (Schweizer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Unique affordances of digital social connection (e.g., impoverished social cues, delayed feedback) have been proposed to confer greater mental health risks, particularly among adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Schweizer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, evidence consistently indicated that face-to-face contact had greater mental health benefits than digital interactions (Bilston et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2024; Stieger et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Indeed, evidence consistently indicated that face-to-face contact had greater mental health benefits than digital interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bilston et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Liang et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Stieger et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Social connection with different partners (e.g., family versus peers) may additionally show differential associations with mental health, especially in adolescents.

Adolescence is marked by a relative shift from predominantly family-based interactions towards more peer-oriented relationships, whereas adulthood which is characterised by more stable networks centred on family and close others (Antonucci et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Adolescence is marked by a relative shift from predominantly family-based interactions towards more peer-oriented relationships, whereas adulthood which is characterised by more stable networks centred on family and close others <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Antonucci et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Although studies have linked greater closeness with family and friends to higher positive affect in older adults (Cavallini et al., 2021), and greater disruptions to peer relationships to mental health difficulties in young people (Magson et al., 2021), developmental differences in changes in social interactions with family versus friends remain underexamined.

text.text: To address these knowledge gaps, the present study utilised data from the multinational COVID-19 Risks Across the Lifespan (CORAL) study.
CORAL is a longitudinal study in individuals, aged 11-89 years which collected social network data thrice.

This permitted examination of age-related differences in social network structure and function and their association with loneliness and depressive symptoms cross-sectionally and prospectively across the first year of the pandemic.
This study used an egocentric network analysis approach, which captures network properties from the respondent's perspective (Burgette et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This study used an egocentric network analysis approach, which captures network properties from the respondent's perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Burgette et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This design allowed for the following hypotheses to be tested: first, social network structure (i.e., density and frequency of contact) and function (i.e., closeness), would vary as a function of age (H1), and greater density and closeness would be associated with fewer symptoms of depression (H2a) and less loneliness (H2b).
These associations (H2) would also vary by age (H3) and across the pandemic (H4).
In addition, less frequent social interactions across modality type (i.e., face-to-face, phone, and other digital means) would be associated with more depressive symptoms and loneliness.

We also explored whether changes from pre-pandemic contact levels were associated with depressive symptoms and loneliness, and whether these associations varied by interaction partner (i.e., with family versus friends) and age.

A total of 3,208 participants were included in the CORAL study who met the inclusion criteria of residing in U.K., U.S., or Australia, fluent in English, (for detailed eligibility criteria see Minihan et al., 2023 Minihan et al., , 2024)).

text.text: For the present study, only individuals with complete age, egocentric social network, mental health, and wellbeing data for at least one study timepoint were included (N = 1,278).
The study was approved by the University of New South Wales Human Research Ethics Committee (HC200287).
All participants provided informed consent, and assent and consent were obtained from parent or guardians for participants under 18 years of age.

Using an egocentric network assessment, participants (also referred to as ego) first reported up to six people (hereafter referred to as alters) with whom they spent the most free time (i.e., time outside of work/school) in person or online.

Participants reported the nature of the relationship for each alter (e.g., mother, friend, husband, sibling), by what means and how often they communicated with each alter, how close they were to each alter and the connections between each alter, including again the type of their relationship (e.g., no connection, relatives, friends) and how close they were to each other.
From this, density, closeness, and frequency of contact were derived (see SI for details on items).
At T1, participants were asked to respond based on experiences in the past year before the COVID-19 pandemic.
They were then also asked to indicate whether the frequency of contact had changed since the onset of the pandemic.
At T2 and T3, responses were based on experiences over the past month.

Density was calculated as the proportion of the number of observed ties relative to the maximum number of possible ties in the network (Burgette et al., 2021; Oliveira & Gama, 2012): n represents the number of alters and aa represents the number of alter-alter ties (i.e., the number of alters that have a connection).
text.formatted: Density was calculated as the proportion of the number of observed ties relative to the maximum number of possible ties in the network <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Burgette et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Oliveira & Gama, 2012)</ref>: n represents the number of alters and aa represents the number of alter-alter ties (i.e., the number of alters that have a connection).

text.text: For a given network size, density is maximised (density = 1) when all possible alter-alter ties are present and minimized when no alter-alter ties exist.
In the present sample, the minimum possible density is 0.286, obtained when a total of 6 alters (n = 6) were reported but no alter-alter ties are present (aa = 0).
Accordingly, observed density values ranged from 0.286 to 1 among participants reporting at least one alter.
Closeness is operationalised as the average strength of all reported connections.
For every reported alter, participants were asked to indicate how close they feel to that alter on a scale of 1 (not close at all) to 10 (extremely close/closer than any other person I know).
The variable 'closeness' referred to the average of these strengths transformed to a scale of 0.1 to 1 ( O'Malley et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The variable 'closeness' referred to the average of these strengths transformed to a scale of 0.1 to 1 ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">O'Malley et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Frequency of contact refers to how often egos interacted with their alters (Huxhold et al., 2013) via three contact modes: 1) face-to-face, 2) interaction by phone, and 3) interaction via other digital means.
text.formatted: Frequency of contact refers to how often egos interacted with their alters <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Huxhold et al., 2013)</ref> via three contact modes: 1) face-to-face, 2) interaction by phone, and 3) interaction via other digital means.

text.text: For each mode, participants indicated how often during the past month they interacted with each alter on a scale of 0 (never) to 4 (every day/ nearly every day).
The mean of frequencies of interactions across all alters was computed for each participant, which resulted in three mean values per participant, one for each contact mode.
This variable had an additional component: at timepoint 1, participants were also asked to indicate how often they interacted with each alter before COVID-19.
This retrospective self-report made it possible to compare the frequency of interaction before COVID-19 and at baseline for each alter.

Average of difference in pre-pandemic and baseline contact-frequency across alters was calculated, and changes in frequency of contact were further separated into contact with family versus friends by averaging across family and friends alters separately.
Depressive symptoms were measured using the 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8; Kroenke et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Depressive symptoms were measured using the 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kroenke et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The eight items asked how often participants were bothered by certain problems (e.g., little interest of pleasure in doing things) on a scale of 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day).
Symptom severity ranged from 0 to 24.
The scale showed good internal consistency at all time points (ωT = 0.93-0.94).
Loneliness was measured using the 20-item UCLA loneliness scale (Russell, 1996).
text.formatted: Loneliness was measured using the 20-item UCLA loneliness scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Russell, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Participants responded to each item (e.g., I have nobody to talk to) on a four-point Likert scale from 0 (I never feel this way) to 3 (I often feel this way).
Total summed loneliness scores ranged from 0-60.
The scale showed excellent internal consistency at all timepoints (ωTs = 0.97).
Analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.0 (R Core Team, 2025).
Detailed model specifications are described in Supplementary Information (SI).
Linear regression models examined crosssectional associations at T1, and linear mixed-effects models examined prospective associations across T1-T3.
Mixed-effects models included time (T1, T2, T3) as a fixed effect and participant ID as a random effect.
For H1, age was included as a fixed effect in separate models for each network index: density, closeness, and frequency of face-to-face, phone, and digital interactions.
H2 models included density, closeness, and their interaction as fixed effects, with depressive symptoms and loneliness modelled as separate outcomes.
H3 extended the H2 models by additionally including age x network index interactions.
Time-interaction effects were included in prospective models for H4.
To account for multiple comparisons, false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied within each hypothesis (e.g., across five models for H1, two models for H2-H4).

For H5, the three types of modalities (face-to-face, phone, and digital means) of contactfrequency were modelled separately as predictors of depressive symptoms and loneliness, resulting in six models.
FDR correction was applied within each outcome, across the three contact-modality models, to avoid over-correction.
Exploratory analyses used the same modelling approach as H5 but replaced raw contactfrequency counts with changes from the pre-pandemic period to T1.
Contact-frequency for family and friends were modelled simultaneously to estimate their relative associations with mental health outcomes.
Age interactions were included in all models to examine age-related differences.
Sensitivity analyses additionally included country as a covariate in the main analysis models to account for differences in COVID-19 policies across the U.K., U.S., and Australia.
The present study included 1,278 participants aged 11-89 years (1,131 females; mean age = 37.2±16.2 years) from the CORAL Study at T1.
T2 and T3 sample Ns were 549 and 471, respectively.

text.text: The present study investigated changes in social connections across the lifespan and their associations with depression and loneliness across the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic.
An egocentric network analysis approach was adopted to examine social connections, whereby participants nominated up to six individuals with whom they spent their free time.
Our findings highlighted key age-related differences, with adolescents reporting more virtual interactions and less in-person interactions than older adults.

Moreover, we found distinct yet complementary associations between structural (i.e., network density) and functional (i.e., network closeness) characteristics of social connections and loneliness, particularly among young people.

Specifically, lower loneliness was reported by individuals with both highly interconnected networks (high density) and strong emotional closeness across social ties, suggesting a joint protective effect.
However, those with highly interconnected but emotionally distant networks reported the highest level of loneliness.

Further, high levels of social contact, particularly face-to-face interactions, were associated with better mental health and less loneliness in adolescents and emerging-to mid-aged adults, during the pandemic.

Exploratory analyses also revealed that disruptions to social connections in the form of reductions in social contact from pre-pandemic levels, across all interaction modes and especially with friends, appeared uniquely damaging to the mental wellbeing of adolescents.
Reduced family contact and its associations with depression and loneliness, however, emerged only later in the pandemic, indicating a potential delayed effect.
Partially consistent with our hypothesis, we observed age-related differences in social interaction frequency, but not in network density or emotional closeness.
Specifically, adolescents reported more frequent virtual contact (i.e., phone and digital) and less frequent face-to-face interactions than older adults.

These patterns are consistent with prior research suggesting a greater preference for virtual social interaction over face-to-face interaction in young people, potentially reflecting the changing norms of social connection in this increasingly digital era (Zheng et al., 2026).

text.text: Greater emotional closeness within one's social network, but not network density, was related to fewer depressive symptoms.

This aligns with research showing that high quality social connections are associated with reduced depressive symptoms in general (Pearce et al., 2023), and particularly during the pandemic (Perry et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023).

text.text: Further, this association persisted across age groups and over the first year of the pandemic, which may reflect the relative stability of closeness as a functional characteristic of social connections across age groups (Bruine de Bruin et al., 2020).

text.text: This highlights the emotional quality of social connections as a potentially important and enduring buffer against depressive symptoms across age and social contexts, including periods of social disruption.
In contrast to depression, loneliness showed a more nuanced relationship with the structural and functional characteristics of social connections during the pandemic.

While greater emotional closeness was generally associated with less reported loneliness, the lowest levels of loneliness were reported by individuals whose social connections were both emotionally close and highly interconnected, indicating a joint protective effect.

Conversely, highly interconnected networks characterised by lower emotional closeness appeared to confer greater risk for loneliness, suggesting that network interconnectedness alone is insufficient to buffer against feelings of social isolation.

This aligns with the notion that mental health benefits from social connections do not come from the mere presence or quantity of social connections, but from their emotional quality (Baumeister & Leary, 1995).

text.text: Notably, these patterns were particularly pronounced among adolescents.
This may be explained by increased social uncertainty in young people (Schweizer et al., 2023), which may heightened further in larger, more interconnected but less emotionally close networks.

text.text: Dense social networks in adolescents likely reflect shared social contexts such as schools and extracurricular contexts.

Abrupt disruptions to these contexts may have disproportionately reduced opportunities for social cues and the affirmation of social connections, partially accounting for the observed marked increases in loneliness among young people during the pandemic (Ernst et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2020).

text.text: However, this is only speculative as social uncertainty was not examined in the present study.

That said, emotionally close social connections appeared to buffer against loneliness despite reduced opportunities for interactions, consistent with research that similarly found perceived social relationship quality protects against loneliness and promotes mental health in adolescents (Cooper et al., 2021).

text.text: Together, these findings highlight that the relationship between loneliness and social connections in adolescents is dependent on both structural and functional properties of their networks, underscoring the need for more nuanced approaches to understanding and addressing the growing loneliness epidemic among young people.

Beyond the structural and functional characteristics of social connections, greater interaction frequency, particularly face-to-face contact, was linked to lower depressive symptoms and loneliness, while more frequent phone contact was specifically linked to lower loneliness.
These findings are consistent with prior research documenting the mental health benefits of social interactions, especially in-person engagement (Liang et al., 2024; Stieger et al., 2023).

text.text: The consistency of these relationships across age and stages of the pandemic highlights frequent, particularly face-to-face, contact as a potential universal target for prevention and intervention across diverse social contexts and demographic groups.

Indeed, interventions aimed at enhancing social functioning (e.g., improving social skills or increasing opportunities for social connection) and social prescription have shown promise in improving mental health outcomes such as loneliness and depression (Hayes et al., 2024; Mitchell et al., 2025).

text.text: However, despite the possible benefits of greater social interaction, this perspective does not fully capture how disruptions or reductions in social contact, such as those experienced during the pandemic, relate to mental health outcomes.

Our results, albeit preliminary, showed that disruptions to social connections, in the form of reduced social contact across all modes (i.e., face-to-face, phone, and digital), were linked to poorer mental wellbeing, both immediately following the pandemic's onset and across the first year.

Further, disruptions to connections with friends were linked to more immediate declines in mental wellbeing, while reduced connection with family was associated with delayed mental health risks later in the pandemic.
Importantly, the mental health risks linked to reduced social contact were again most pronounced among adolescents, and to a lesser extent, among emerging-to mid-aged adults.

While this may partly reflect a greater reliance on social connections for mental wellbeing in adolescents (Orben et al., 2020), it also underscores the importance of safeguarding social connections in contexts characterised by reductions in social contact (e.g., educational transitions, relocation, institutionalisation, forced displacement, and natural disasters), particularly for young people.

text.text: The present study has several methodological strengths including the use of large, multinational, prospective data collected across the first-year of the pandemic.
However, results should be considered in light of the following limitations.

First, despite efforts to recruit participants with diverse demographic backgrounds across three countries, the use of convenience sampling resulted in a sample comprised primarily of Caucasian females, thus limiting the generalisability of the findings given documented differences in social connections across gender (Friebel et al., 2021) and cultural contexts (Igarashi et al., 2008).
text.formatted: First, despite efforts to recruit participants with diverse demographic backgrounds across three countries, the use of convenience sampling resulted in a sample comprised primarily of Caucasian females, thus limiting the generalisability of the findings given documented differences in social connections across gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Friebel et al., 2021)</ref> and cultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Igarashi et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Second, although the present study identified important age-related differences and temporal variance in associations between disruptions to social connections and mental wellbeing, the underlying mechanisms remain unexplored.
Future studies should further investigate explanatory factors, such as coping strategies (Geçer & Yıldırım, 2023), to better inform the development of targeted intervention and prevention efforts.
text.formatted: Future studies should further investigate explanatory factors, such as coping strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Geçer & Yıldırım, 2023)</ref>, to better inform the development of targeted intervention and prevention efforts.

text.text: Third, the present study considered average network density, emotional closeness, and frequency of interaction across one to six social connections but did not account for the stability of social relationships across assessment timepoints.

For example, individuals who report on the same connections at all timepoints may be considered to have more stable relationships than those who report on different connections, which may have differing implications for their mental health outcomes.

Finally, for feasibility reasons, the study employed an egocentric network analysis approach, which captures social connections from the perspective of the individual respondent, as opposed to a sociocentric approach that constructs network structures based on reports from all members within a network (Burgette et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Finally, for feasibility reasons, the study employed an egocentric network analysis approach, which captures social connections from the perspective of the individual respondent, as opposed to a sociocentric approach that constructs network structures based on reports from all members within a network <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Burgette et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, our findings may be influenced by subjectivity and recall bias.

However, given recent evidence highlighting the importance of subjective social experiences for mental health, this approach may be particularly relevant for understanding mental wellbeing outcomes (Nasirpour et al., 2025; Piera Pi-Sunyer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, given recent evidence highlighting the importance of subjective social experiences for mental health, this approach may be particularly relevant for understanding mental wellbeing outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Nasirpour et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Piera Pi-Sunyer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, future studies adopting a sociocentric approach could provide a more comprehensive understanding of how objective and subjective characteristics of social connections, independently and/or jointly, relate to mental health.
Across the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, disruptions to social connection were consistently associated with poorer mental health and greater loneliness.
These associations were strongest among adolescents, suggesting that social network disruption may represent an important developmental risk factor for mental wellbeing.

The findings highlight the distinct yet complementary roles of structural and functional characteristics of social connections, as well as the importance of both high interaction frequency and reductions in social contact in shaping mental wellbeing outcomes.
Together, these findings have important implications for informing age-sensitive strategies to support mental wellbeing, particularly among young people.
